# **Serious Game Project: MVP Design Document**

You've identified your topic, tested three different game perspectives, and playtested with real players. Now you're going to document your game in detail before you build it digitally. This design document is your blueprint. It shows what your game looks like, how it works, and why each part matters.

Your design document should have:

* A clear description of your chosen paper prototype  
* Sketches and descriptions of your game screens and mechanics  
* Justification for why this design serves your learning goal

---

## **Part 1 \- Your Game at a Glance**

**Sentence 1:** We are making a game about \[topic\] for \[audience\], because they are the people who most need to understand it.

| We are making a game about thrifting for teenagers, because they are the people who are influenced the most by trends, especially in fashion. |
| :---- |

**Sentence 2 \- Learning Goal:** We want a player to walk away understanding \[one specific thing\]. 

| We want a player to walk away understanding the impacts fast fashion has on lower income countries and the positive impact of reusing and giving away old clothes. |
| :---- |

## **Part 2 \- Choose Your Paper Prototype**

**Choose (and refine) your best paper prototype. Add pictures of it here:**

| ![][image1] ![][image2] ![][image3] ![][image4] ![][image5] |
| :---- |

**Describe how to play your paper prototype.**

| You walk into the corporate building with a plan to take down the CEO and ultimately the company to save the planet. As you walk in, workers detect you as a threat and attempt to stop you from going any further. You fight them with your basic hand to hand combat skills and you win\! A clothing rack drops from the ceiling as your reward and you choose between 3 different outfits with unknown abilities. You ascend the tower and defeat the CEO. You have saved the planet\!\!\!\!\!\! |
| :---- |

**What made this prototype work?** Describe one moment from playtesting that showed you this was the right direction. What did a playtester do or say?

| It was the most well-designed because we spent the most time creating it and refining it. A moment from playtesting that showed us this was when Miles finished the game. He asked if he could play again so he could try the other outfits out. |
| :---- |

## **Part 3 \- Mechanics, Dynamics, Aesthetics**

These three things work together to create your game experience.

**What is your most important mechanic?** The rule or action. (Example: "The player chooses which person to help with limited time per turn.")

| Choosing your clothing to best combat the enemies and look nice too. |
| :---- |

**What dynamic should this elicit?** What happens as a result? What tension or situation does the mechanic create? (Example: "The player faces real tension because they can't help everyone.")

| The player feels in power and like they could make a difference in stopping climate change. |
| :---- |

**What aesthetic should players feel?** What do you want it to feel like to play? (Example: "Stress. Moral weight. The feeling of helplessness in the face of competing needs.")

| The player should feel motivation to beat up all the enemies, accomplishment from completing a floor, and empowerment from getting new gear and abilities |
| :---- |

**How do these three work together to serve your learning goal?**

| All of the aesthetics come from the mechanics of choice, giving the player the freedom to try new things out, and the dynamic helps with the image because he player dictates what they can do and how they look. |
| :---- |

---

## **Part 4 \- Mechanics and Story Alignment**

Now let’s flesh out your paper prototype into a game idea\! In a serious game, your mechanics should embody your message, not just decorate it.

**What story are you telling?** Briefly describe the scenario, the world, or the situation the player enters.

| The world is overrun by fast fashion and 1 million percent polyester clothes lie in piles in the streets. Smog pollutes the sky from nearby clothing factories. 5 clothing companies run the world and lobby the government. The top 0.0001% own 90% of wealth. The player wants change for his community and vies to defeat the companies. |
| :---- |

**How do your mechanics embody this story?** Don't explain it through dialogue or cutscenes. Explain it through what the player actually does. Why does that specific action matter thematically?

| As the player defeats enemies, they earn clothing. Each outfit has trade-offs, like some clothing are powerful but leak microplastics into your body, making you weaker the longer you have it on. Other outfits are thrifted or reused and are more sustainable. The player has to balance strength with environmental considerations which fits our fast fashion theme. |
| :---- |

---

## **Part 5 \- Goals, Subgoals, and Pacing**

**Overall goal:** What is the player trying to accomplish? This should connect to your learning goal.

| The player is trying to save the environment. |
| :---- |

**Subgoals:** What are 2-4 smaller objectives the player works toward on the way to the overall goal? (List them in order.)

| The player is trying to defeat one fast fashion company (one at a time) The player is trying to get the best gear possible The player is trying to clear the current company floor they are on. The player is trying to defeat the enemy currently opposing them (like a basic enemy) |
| :---- |

**Pacing:** How does the game get harder or more complex? When does the player feel successful? When do they feel challenged? You can sketch a quick graph, describe it, or both.

| The game gets harder by throwing tougher and tougher enemies and you need more complex outfits which have abilities that synergize together, thus multiplying their total damage output. The player feels sucessful when they beat tough enemies and build cool outfits with unique abilities. They feel challenged when deciding which outfits would work best for their playstyle or when fighting enemies. |
| :---- |

## **Part 7 \- Sketch Your MVG**

Sketch out everything that will be needed for your “Minimum Viable Game.” Rough sketches are better than no sketches. These don't need to be pretty.

**What does the player see on screen?** Sketch the **minimum** different views for your game to work. 

|   ![][image11]  |
| :---- |

**What are the UI elements?** (Player character, enemies, items, obstacles, buttons, counters, timers, text, icons, etc. What’s the **minimum** that the player would need to see and interact with?)

| There is a health bar, life bar, money currently held, and inventory slots in the top left (only the health bar and money held is necessary). The floors completed are in the top right with an image of the building you're on. The player is fighting an enemy with a fire blast. Also ignore how the fire is the wrong way.  |
| :---- |

**How does the game communicate?** How does the player know what happened? (Visual feedback, sounds, text, numbers, images?)

| The health & life bar gives you feedback as to how many times you have been hit and how close to failing you are. The enemy is also being knocked back to show the impact of your attack. In our final game we’ll have damage numbers pop up when receiving or dealing damage, the screen will flash red when you take damage, and the enemies/player will look better then how they currently do.  |
| :---- |
